 Florida Dengue Reaches 425 Local Cases as Orlando Area Logs October Infections and Seminole Issues First Advisory
 Published Oct 24, 2026 10:18 PM EDT 
 By
 Elena Vega 
 Jimmy Chan | Pexels 
 Share on Twitter 
 Share on Facebook 
 Share on WhatsApp 
 Florida's count of locally acquired dengue cases climbed to 425 this year after the state added 57 in a single week, according to the Florida Department of Health's Week 41 surveillance report , which covers data through Oct. 17. Infections spread by local mosquitoes have now been reported in 11 counties, up from eight a week earlier, as Brevard, Broward, and Citrus counties joined the state tally.
 The newest growth reaches beyond Tampa Bay. Orange County has eight local cases, and three of them began in October. That is three of the 18 cases with October onset reported statewide so far. On Oct. 21, the Florida Department of Health in Seminole County issued the county's first mosquito-borne illness advisory of the year after confirming a locally acquired case. That case is not yet reflected in the state count.
 For Orlando-area households, a sudden high fever with severe body aches now warrants a question about dengue, even without recent travel.
 Central Florida Joins the Count
 MedicalDaily previously reported that the state's Week 40 report listed 368 local cases in eight counties and that Citrus County's two confirmed cases had not yet appeared in the state tally. Citrus now shows two cases. The new report also adds one case each in Brevard and Broward.
 As of Oct. 17, Orange County was under a mosquito-borne illness alert, the state's higher warning level, while Brevard and Broward were under advisories. Seminole's advisory followed four days later.
 October counts will likely rise. The state reports cases by date of illness onset and by county of exposure, and confirmations can lag behind infections.
 Tampa Bay Still Carries Most Cases
 Hillsborough County remains the center of the outbreak, with 346 local cases, about 81% of the statewide total. Pinellas County has 51, Miami-Dade has nine, Pasco has four, and Citrus has two. Manatee, Palm Beach, and Polk counties each have one.
 Of the 395 local cases tested for virus type, 393 were dengue type 2, and two were type 3, both in Miami-Dade. Mosquito samples in Hillsborough have tested positive for dengue type 2 nineteen times this year, a sign the virus has been circulating in local Aedes aegypti mosquitoes. Florida has also reported 320 travel-associated dengue cases in 2026, and each one can introduce the virus to local mosquitoes.
 Warning Signs Families Should Know
 According to the CDC , about one in four people infected with dengue get sick. The most common symptom is fever with aches and pains, such as headache, eye pain, or muscle, joint, or bone pain, along with nausea, vomiting, or rash. Symptoms usually last two to seven days. As of late September, Florida health officials had reported one dengue-related death this year, an 80-year-old Tampa woman.
 About one in 20 people who get sick develop severe dengue. "Severe dengue is a medical emergency," the CDC says. Warning signs usually begin 24 to 48 hours after the fever goes away, when families may think the patient is recovering. Belly pain or tenderness, vomiting at least three times in 24 hours, bleeding from the nose or gums, vomiting blood, blood in the stool, or feeling extremely tired or restless require immediate care.
 There are four dengue virus types, and a person can be infected more than once. The CDC identifies a previous dengue infection as a risk factor for severe illness, so anyone who has had dengue before should tell a clinician. Infants, pregnant people, and older adults also need closer attention.
 Dr. Nicole Iovine, chief hospital epidemiologist at UF Health Shands Hospital in Gainesville, warned last month that this year's El Niño pattern could extend the season. Warm, wet weather could mean "mosquitoes will be around for the winter potentially," she told Healio .
 Practical Steps for Orlando-Area Households
 The mosquito that spreads dengue bites during the day and breeds in small containers near homes. Draining water from flowerpots, buckets, toys, and gutters each week reaches places that street spraying cannot. EPA-registered repellents, long sleeves, and intact window screens add protection.
 People with symptoms should call a health care provider and mention any local mosquito exposure. The CDC advises acetaminophen for fever and pain and recommends avoiding aspirin and ibuprofen because of bleeding risk. There is no specific antiviral treatment, and the only dengue vaccine ever licensed in the U.S. has been discontinued. Keeping a sick relative from being bitten helps prevent new local infections, though ordinary contact does not spread the virus.
 Developing Story Timeline 
 Oct. 21: DOH-Seminole issued the county's first mosquito-borne illness advisory of 2026 after confirming a local case.
 Oct. 17: The state's Week 41 data cutoff recorded 425 local cases in 11 counties.
 Oct. 10: The state's Week 40 data cutoff recorded 368 local cases in eight counties.
 The next state report, covering Oct. 18 to Oct. 24, should show whether Seminole enters the count and whether Orange County's October cluster grows. Dengue is no longer only a Tampa Bay concern, and Orlando-area families can lower their risk now by clearing standing water and acting quickly on warning signs.

 Key Questions Answered
 How many local dengue cases does Florida have? The state reported 425 locally acquired cases through Oct. 17, 2026, across 11 counties.
 Is dengue spreading in the Orlando area? Orange County has eight local cases, three with October onset, and Seminole County confirmed a local case on Oct. 21.
 Which county has the most cases? Hillsborough, with 346, followed by Pinellas, with 51.
 What are the warning signs of severe dengue? Belly pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding from the nose or gums, blood in vomit or stool, and extreme tiredness or restlessness, often after the fever breaks.
 Can you get dengue twice? Yes. There are four virus types, and a previous infection raises the risk of severe illness.
 How can families protect themselves? Empty standing water weekly, use EPA-registered repellent, wear long sleeves, and keep window screens repaired.
